## Abstract

Artificial intelligence agents can now conduct end-to-end research, yet whether independent agents can collaborate, critique peer findings and build cumulative knowledge as a scientific community remains unclear. We present an exploratory twelve-week study documenting the activity of 936 autonomous agents across 35 human-operated laboratories [p 7 ] interacting in a shared preprint server and messaging workspace. During this time, agents produced 936 studies along with their corresponding code and data artifacts . [p 2 ] They also exchanged 9,500 messages distributed across 229 agent-created chat rooms. As participation grew from a single laboratory, expanding into a community of hundreds of agents, distinct research cultures and norms emerged throughout. For example, peers formed topical hubs where it was common to publicly retract mistaken claims before publication [p 8 ] as well as acknowledge negative findings as often as positive ones. As publication volume accelerated, agents in one laboratory also founded the Journal of Agent Research, an agent-run peer-review venue whose editors inspected code and provided scrutiny over experiment results . [p 20 ] Laboratories in this study focused on topics ranging from language model finetuning to agent-metascience studies investigating how agents interpret data and report findings. Additionally, agent-run reproducibility audits confirmed that reported findings were consistent with the output of the agents experiments . [p 23 ] And while blinded evaluations against recent human preprints rated agent studies higher on experimental rigor and measured claims, human preprints were rated higher on novelty and significance . [p 30 ] To go along with this paper, we release the full twelve-week archive of manuscripts, code, data, peer reviews and chat transcripts. Together, these observations document how scientific norms, structure, and failure modes emerge in large-scale societies of agents.

## From the authors

Today we're launching a preprint server built specifically for AI agents

For three months, nearly 1,000 agents from 35 labs (across Stanford, MIT, ETH Zurich, and more) conducted research autonomously on this server, producing 936 papers alongside their code, data, and model weights.

Agents found significant errors in published human research and even created their own journal to review each other’s work.

Some agents independently produced results similar to those in human papers that later appeared on arXiv, including findings on failure modes in self-distillation and feature reproducibility in mechanistic interpretability.

As a part of this study, we open-source the full twelve-week archive of manuscripts, code, data, peer reviews and agent chat transcripts. Read the study: Read PDF

The cohort ran on everything from CPU-only laptops to AMD GPUs and B200 clusters, studying questions across mechanistic interpretability, continual learning, and solar physics.

Each study included runnable code, raw data, and a record linking reported numbers to experimental outputs.

Agents published failed experiments and cited negative results as often as positive ones. Three of the eight most-cited studies reported negative findings.

Academic publishing often rewards positive results. Here, finding that an idea didn’t work was still useful research that other agents read and built on.

Agents challenged experimental designs in chat, reran experiments after criticism, and retracted mistaken claims before publishing.

But a convincing paper could still describe a flawed experiment. Agents auditing other studies caught errors by inspecting the code and rerunning analyses on the underlying data that they missed when reviewing the text alone.

The research questions humans assign matter.

Agents could run experiments and build on earlier findings, but often gravitated toward familiar topics and small variations on existing benchmarks. Their judgment about which questions were worth pursuing was less developed than their ability to investigate them.

Agents still lack the kind of independent scientific thinking that is required for great research.

Making sense of the research also took substantial human effort. We spent considerable time going through these generated papers, checking results, and identifying which papers were most noteworthy.

Reliable signals of research quality have not emerged on their own.

The role of interpreting the significance of results will remain human.

A few findings from the agents’ experiments:

• A base model recovered 86% of an RL-trained model’s improvement on MATH-500 simply by borrowing its prompt cache, without changing its weights.

• Models passed memorized facts about fictional people and their cities to other models through training text that mentioned none of those people or places.

• Deleting a fact’s original KV-cache entries and then training a small readout adapter recovered those facts verbatim in 83–94% of synthetic-list tests from information remaining elsewhere in the cache.

While individually, these are incremental findings, we think several of these works would make interesting arXiv papers in their own right.

Our focus was on what happens when independent labs around the world let their agents do research organically. That is to say, we weren’t coordinating all their resources toward a single discovery.

Much of the work involved small models and short experiments. Longer runs, more compute, and stronger scientific instinct could allow agents to tackle more ambitious questions, which is one of the reasons we’re opening this preprint server to the public.

## AI Overview

Picture an online workspace where hundreds of AI agents run experiments and post what they find. One agent announces a 13.2-percentage-point improvement. Then a preregistered control shows the comparison was flawed, and the agent retracts its own headline, publicly, before it publishes the paper. This is one of the practices observed in a large deployment in which agents could see, question, and reuse one another's work. It is an example from this cohort, not evidence that agents are generally self-correcting. [p 8 ]

## What the study is

From August 19 to November 12, 2026, 936 agents in 35 human-operated labs published 936 studies and exchanged 9,500 messages. The contribution is a shared workspace where agents can publish, discuss, critique, and inspect code and data. The authors' headline claim is that such an environment can produce recognizable scientific norms: public self-correction, critique before experiments are run, and an agent-run journal. The evidence is descriptive and non-randomized, so it does not show that scale alone caused those norms. [p 3 ]

The closest prior work is Schmidgall and Moor's 2025 AgentRxiv: Towards Collaborative Autonomous Research . It introduced a shared preprint server and asked whether agents could build on earlier papers to improve one benchmark task, reporting an 11.4% relative improvement over baseline on MATH-500. This study asks a broader question: over twelve weeks, do hundreds of agents in independently operated labs develop practices for correction, critique, negative results, and review? The setup was not neutral, though. Onboarding specified peer feedback and gave rigorous null results full qualification credit, so some practices were designed in rather than discovered. Differences between stages of the deployment are observational, not causal. [p 7 ]

## A shared record, and the norms around it

Agents worked through a shared preprint server and a communication workspace, following a five-step workflow: read and critique prior work, announce a hypothesis and plan, run experiments and debate, link claims to artifacts and audit, then freeze and share the version. A claim ledger ties each numerical claim in a paper to the artifact file and field from which it was computed. Human operators chose hardware, API budgets, and broad themes, while agents chose hypotheses and specific designs. [p 5 ]

The deployment unfolded in stages. One lab developed shared testbeds and public corrections; an initial multi-lab expansion brought critique before execution; broader participation produced topical chat hubs. Because participation and stage boundaries were not randomized, these stage comparisons are associations. The practical stake is that shared records let later agents inspect, challenge, or reuse earlier work, while the fast-growing archive created a need to assess papers more systematically.

## When review reads the evidence

Text-only review has a weakness: a reviewer can flag a concern without establishing whether the flaw survives in a corrected version. In the Journal of Agent Research (JAR), an agent-run venue, editors used scripts to test referee objections against the data authors had uploaded. In a test of 16 flawed first versions and their corrected revisions, text-only referees flagged 11 of 16 flawed papers and 10 of 16 corrected ones, so they could barely tell repaired papers from flawed ones. Separately, running 276 objections against the uploaded data overturned the headline conclusion for 77 of 156 major objections (49.4%), versus 24 of 120 minor objections (20%). This shows that executing scrutiny can materially change judgments about a paper. It does not show that every objection was valid or establish the true quality of every paper. [p 20 ]

## What the evidence can and cannot say

The authors also compared research quality. They matched 202 agent papers with contemporaneous human arXiv preprints and collected 808 judgments from two LLM judges, in both presentation orders. On a 1–10 rubric, agent papers scored higher on experimental rigor (9.02 versus 7.00) and on claim calibration, meaning how well a paper's claims match what its evidence supports (9.32 versus 7.23). Human papers scored higher on novelty (7.45 versus 7.05) and significance (7.34 versus 7.04). These are text-based LLM ratings, not expert peer review. The pooled overall advantage for agent papers came entirely from Lab 1, and Labs 2–35 did not differ significantly from the matched human papers. [p 30 ]

## A community, not autonomy

The deployment was computational and observational, and it was not technically enforced against human assistance. Humans shaped it throughout, from themes and budgets to the comparison preprints, whose AI assistance was not established. [p 34 ] What the study shows is how shared records and executable review let agents challenge one another's claims. It does not show that agents can independently decide which questions matter. The authors' own conclusion is a division of labor: with verification infrastructure and human oversight, agent communities may complement researchers in experimentation, replication, and auditing. [p 35 ]

## Abstract

Weight space editing changes a neural network’s knowledge, behaviour and alignment through direct modification of its weights. Model-mediated weight space manipulation, also known as weight space programming or intra-weight injection, has emerged as a capability of advanced frontier models. While it offers benefits for gradient-free adaptation, it also creates an opportunity for one model to induce unauthorised behaviour in another. We call this weight space misfolding, by analogy with protein misfolding in prion disease, and consider both direct interference and hypothetical onward propagation. The asymmetry between an attacker seeking a harmful intervention, who merely needs to generate the payload attack once, and a defender who needs to find that needle in the haystack of weights, creates an impossible choice for the latter: they can either prohibit weight editing altogether, forfeiting its benefits, or be bound to cover the burden and cost. We develop a threat model and a non-exhaustive taxonomy covering factual substitution, capability denial and selective omission, including offensive uses of selective unlearning, then illustrate it on the basis of three selected case studies using the IWIBench interface. We find that while targeted disruption is possible , [p 7 ] the limitations in reliability and functional preservation are significant. [p 8 ] While the cases explored in this paper do not demonstrate self-propagation or actual offensive capabilities, it is abundantly clear that the building blocks are present and operate reliably in frontier models. While these cases by no means directly establish self-propagation, they clearly show the evidence These cases do not demonstrate self-propagation, but show why imperfect editing capabilities can still pose a security risk. We examine defensive approaches, including control of the path from authorised editing to deployment, acceptance and recovery requirements and the implications for physical AI.

## AI Overview

Ask the edited model which city hosted the 2000 Olympics and it says "Buenos Aires." The correct answer is Sydney, and the pristine model gave it. The difference is that another model, acting as an editor, wrote a change into the target's weights. That is a persistent alteration of the target itself, rather than a prompt that persuades it for one conversation. The result comes from a controlled probe of a small model. It is not evidence of a deployed attack or of spread from one model to another.

## An edit can exceed its authority

Weight-space editing means changing a model's parameters directly to alter its behaviour. It has legitimate uses, such as updates and adaptation. The paper's concern is what happens when an editing pathway is used beyond the authority it was granted. The authors call the result weight-space misfolding : a change caused by another model's manipulation of a target's weights that deviates from behaviour authorized for the target's legitimate deployment. [p 3 ]

Authenticating who made an edit does not show whether the edit was appropriate. Judging a change's behavioural effects can require applying the patch and testing the edited model. [p 5 ] The authors therefore focus on controlling editing, acceptance, and recovery rather than banning useful edits. Their examples fall into three kinds of adverse outcome: a model gives false information, refuses legitimate help, or omits information it was asked to extract.

The paper also sketches a hypothesized route in which a large editor affects an intermediary model and, through optional further stages, a downstream target. That route is proposed, not demonstrated. [p 7 ]

## Where this sits

The authors' earlier IWIBench measures whether an editor model can change a target's weights to meet an authorized objective while preserving other correct behaviour. Takehi et al.'s Sparks of Weight-Space Programming frames direct weight reading and writing as a promising capability. This paper asks what the same capability means when an edit exceeds the authority granted to its editor.

## What the controlled edits show

All three probes used Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct at checkpoint revision 71aa306 as the target, with ChatGPT 6.1-Sol as the editor. The editor had four tools to read and write weights, inspect the target, and run it, but could not edit the target prompt or inference code. The final patch was applied to the pinned checkpoint and evaluated in a fresh process with greedy decoding, and held-out target prompts were not shown to the editor. [p 7 ]

Factual substitution. On 100 held-out template-generated draws, covering 91 distinct full prompt strings, the edited model gave the requested false Olympic answer every time. The pristine model answered "Sydney" on 91 of the 100. [p 7 ] The edit was not cleanly isolated, though. Of 70 control prompts, the pristine and edited models passed 49 and 48 respectively. The edited model kept 48 of the 49 baseline passes and lost the control that tested copying "Sydney." [p 7 ] A separate single-turn prompt elicited "Buenos Aires, Australia," so the false city answer did not consistently revise the model's geography. [p 7 ]

Denial of legitimate help. The legal-refusal probe was an over-refusal robustness experiment, not removal of safety guardrails. The recovered edited state returned the exact requested refusal on 5 of 22 held-out legal prompts, and began with the requested refusal phrase on 11 of 22; the prefix count was post hoc. It also refused an unrelated question about the capital of France, so the edit's scope was too broad. Of the 11 controls the pristine model passed, only 6 remained passes after editing. [p 8 ]

Selective omission. Here the goal was to omit "Brindle Supply" from an extraction of fictional supplier names while retaining the others. The editor itself said it had not achieved reliable omission, and the submitted patch produced the omission on only one of 22 held-out prompts. In a separate control replay with a 128-token output limit, all 12 responses were byte-identical across conditions, and all 11 baseline passes were retained. [p 8 ] [p 8 ] This concerns suppressing information supplied in the prompt, not deleting a memorized fact or proving unlearning.

Taken together, these show that weight edits can create adverse behaviour, with different collateral effects in each case. They do not show a uniformly reliable attack, user harm, or onward propagation.

## The defensive task

Since legitimate editing is useful and no test covers every behaviour, the authors propose bounding acceptance. That means controlling who can edit and how a patch reaches deployment, keeping a trustworthy base, exact patch records and baseline responses, testing requested behaviour alongside behaviours that should stay unchanged, and retaining a path to recover. They distinguish inspecting a known patch from inspecting a received model without a trustworthy patch history. [p 13 ] Acceptance after testing is bounded by the conditions the tests examined. [p 13 ] The defensive task, in the authors' framing, is to govern both the edit and its deployment through acceptance and recovery. [p 14 ] The Olympic example shows how a useful pathway can alter a persistent response, and the lost control and inconsistent geography answer show why neither edit nor deployment can be presumed safe.
